title: Assigning a variable to itself
summary: Why `name = name` can leave a field unchanged, and how to tell which variable an assignment uses.
objectives: Explain what `=` does and which way a value is copied.
Explain how a constructor parameter can hide a field with the same name.
Trace what changes and what stays the same in `name = name`.
Fix the bug by assigning the parameter to the field.

bad.title: Assigns the parameter to itself

good.title: Assigns the parameter to the field

blocks.note: In the first version, both uses of `name` refer to the constructor parameter. The field does not get the parameter's value. In the fixed version, `this.name` means the field belonging to this object.

blocks.title: This is a run-time bug
blocks.text: Both versions are valid Java, so `javac` accepts them. The mistake usually has no compiler warning. The bad value becomes visible when the program runs and reads the field.

A constructor parameter is a local variable: it belongs to the constructor call. A field belongs to an object. When a parameter and a field have the same name, using just `name` inside the constructor refers to the parameter. The field begins as `null`, Java's default value for a field whose type is `String`.

blocks.caption: What `name = name` refers to
blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A[Constructor begins] --> B[Parameter name holds Ava]
  B --> C[Read parameter name on the right]
  C --> D[Write parameter name on the left]
  D --> E[Field name stays null]
  E --> F[Use this.name to name the field]

blocks.title: Read an assignment from right to left
blocks.text: In `left = right`, Java copies the value on the right into the variable on the left. So `name = name` copies the parameter's value back into that same parameter. It does not copy anything into the field.
Suppose the constructor receives `"Ava"`. Follow each name in the broken assignment. The parameter and field are separate places, even though they have the same name.

blocks.caption: Tracing `name = name` when the constructor receives `"Ava"`
rows: The field has its default value.
The left-side `name` is also the parameter.

blocks.text: The assignment leaves the parameter with the same value it already had. It never mentions `this.name`, so the field stays `null`.
Here is a complete program using the student's pattern. The getter returns the field so we can see what the constructor stored.

bad.title: Broken constructor prints null

good.title: Fixed constructor prints Ava

blocks.note: In the broken program, the getter reads the field, which still holds `null`. In the fixed program, `this.name = name` copies the parameter into the field.

blocks.text: The same mistake can happen with a number field. An `int` field starts with the default value `0` if the constructor does not change it.

bad.title: The age field stays 0

good.title: The age field becomes 19

blocks.note: The parameter receives `19`, but `age = age` only assigns the parameter to itself. The field remains at its default value, `0`. Adding `this.` makes the left side the field.

blocks.caption: Age stored in the field after construction

blocks.text: The key clue is not the word `name`. The bug can use any field and parameter with the same name. Check which variable each side of `=` refers to.

bad.title: A setter changes only its parameter

blocks.note: A setter is a method meant to change a field. In the bad version, the field is not changed, just as in the constructor.

bad.title: A field and parameter share a name

good.title: Make the field clear on the left

blocks.note: The field `count` and parameter `count` are different variables. `this.count` identifies the field. The same issue can occur in methods as well as constructors.

blocks.question: In this constructor, which variable does the left-side `name` refer to?
blocks.explanation: The parameter has the same name as the field, so the unqualified `name` refers to the parameter inside the constructor. Use `this.name` to refer to the field.

blocks.question: A field `age` and a parameter `age` both exist. Which assignment stores the parameter's value in the field?
blocks.explanation: `this.age` is the field, and the unqualified `age` on the right is the parameter. The `=` operator copies the right-side value into the left-side variable.

blocks.question: What does the field print after this constructor runs?
options: The value passed to the constructor
blocks.explanation: The assignment changes only the parameter. The `int` field is never assigned, so it keeps its default value, `0`. The constructor is valid Java and the mistake is not rejected by the compiler.

items: In `left = right`, Java copies the right-side value into the left-side variable.
A constructor parameter and a field are separate variables, even when they have the same name.
In `name = name`, both names refer to the parameter, so the field stays unchanged.
Use `this.name = name` to copy a parameter into the object's `name` field.
This mistake is valid Java. The wrong field value appears when the program runs, not as a compiler error.
